summary: Describes a possible strategy for testing implementations of RTP, the real-time transport protocol.

eli5.summary: It's a plan for checking that a live-audio program works correctly.

subtitle: Testing strategies for real-time audio and video streaming protocol implementations.

tldr.problem: RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol) implementations vary widely and interoperability is not guaranteed. There is no standard test suite to verify that implementations are correct or can work together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a testing architecture using a test instrument that forwards packets between two RTP implementations while simulating network conditions (delays, packet loss). It outlines tests for media transport, RTCP control packets, timing behavior, translators, mixers, and SSRC randomization.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can use this test strategy to verify their RTP implementations are correct, demonstrate interoperability, and identify common implementation errors before deployment.

facts.label: RTCP packet randomization
facts.value: Not constant; uniformly distributed within computed interval

today: RFC 3158 is an Informational RFC that describes testing strategies for RTP implementations. It remains relevant for developers implementing RTP and testing interoperability, though it references earlier drafts of RTP specifications.

sections.title: Overview and Testing Architecture
sections.content:
RTP is the standard protocol for real-time audio and video streaming on the Internet. However, the specification is complex, and implementations vary in correctness and completeness. Without a standardized test strategy, verifying interoperability is difficult.

This RFC does not mandate a test suite that implementations MUST pass. Instead, it describes a testing strategy to help developers verify their implementations and demonstrate interoperability. Tests are categorized by the aspect being verified: end systems, translators (which change encoding), and mixers (which combine multiple sources).

The basic test architecture uses three machines on a local network: two running RTP implementations being tested, and a third running a test instrument that acts as a transparent packet forwarder. The test instrument can delay or discard packets to simulate poor network conditions, log packet contents for inspection, and send crafted packets to the implementations.

Tests cover edge cases that proper implementations must handle correctly, such as sequence number and timestamp wrap-around, the marker bit, padding, header extensions, and unsupported payload types.
sections.eli5: You set up two streaming apps talking through a test machine. The test machine watches if they do things right: sending packets correctly, handling delays and lost packets, and following the rules.

sections.title: Media Transport and RTCP Testing
sections.content:
Media Transport Tests: The first test has one implementation send RTP data packets while the other receives. The test verifies the receiver correctly handles edge cases: padding in packets, the marker bit set, wrap-around of sequence numbers (after 65535 packets) and timestamps, different payload types, and unsupported payload types. The sender is verified to choose random initial values for SSRC, sequence number, and timestamp; increment sequence number by one for each packet; and correctly handle wrap-around.

Basic RTCP Tests: While both implementations run but neither sends data, they should generate RTCP control packets. The test verifies these are compound packets starting with an empty RR (receiver report), and containing an SDES CNAME item. When one implementation sends data, it should generate SR (sender report) packets instead of RR packets, and the receiver should generate RR packets. Tests verify correct fields in SR and RR packets: SSRC consistency, NTP and RTP timestamps, packet and octet counts, and reception quality metrics (loss fraction, jitter, last sender report timestamp, delay since last SR).

RTCP Compound Packet Structure: Implementations must correctly format RTCP as compound packets. Tests verify the length field matches packet length, the RC (report count) field is correct, and timestamps align across packets.

Stress tests introduce packet loss (dropping 1% of packets) and random delays. The implementation must handle this gracefully, with RR packets correctly reporting loss fraction and cumulative packet loss increasing over time. Jitter reporting should increase with added delays.
sections.eli5: Tests check if one app sends packets right, the other receives them right, they exchange control reports properly, and they handle lost or late packets correctly.

sections.title: RTCP Timing and Advanced Behaviors
sections.content:
RTCP Transmission Interval Tests: RTP uses a complex algorithm to determine when to send RTCP packets. A minimum interval of 5 seconds (for receivers) is enforced to avoid flooding. For large groups, the interval scales up. Senders use a different (smaller) minimum interval than receivers. A test implementation becomes a single receiver on a LAN, transmits no data, but receives crafted RTCP packets from the test instrument. The implementation should generate RTCP packets with correct randomization: minimum interval between 2-2.5 seconds, maximum between 5.5-7 seconds, average around 5 seconds, and randomization that is non-uniform (not constant intervals).

Step Join Backoff: When many participants suddenly join a session, the reconsideration algorithm must prevent a flood of RTCP packets. A test sends 100 RTCP packets (simulating 100 new participants) to the implementation and measures delay until the next RTCP packet. With reconsideration, this delay should follow a specific formula based on group size and bandwidth. Without reconsideration, the delay would be much shorter.

Reverse Reconsideration and BYE Handling: When group membership drops (participants leave via BYE packets), the interval should decrease more rapidly than increase (reverse reconsideration). BYE reconsideration tests verify that when the implementation leaves the group, it sends a BYE packet (or none) within the correct time window, not immediately or excessively delayed.

Timeout and Rapid RTCP: Implementations must time out participants who don't send RTCP for 5 intervals. For high-bandwidth sessions, implementations should use a reduced minimum RTCP interval (as low as 0.5 seconds). Tests verify correct timeout behavior and reduced interval support.
sections.eli5: The protocol has rules about how often each app sends status messages. Tests check if apps follow these timing rules: not sending too often, speeding up when people join, slowing down when people leave, and forgetting people who go silent.

sections.title: Translators, Mixers and SSRC Handling
sections.content:
Translator Testing: A translator receives RTP from one source, converts the encoding or format, and forwards to another implementation. The translator should preserve the SSRC (source identifier) of the original sender, set CC (CSRC count) to zero, and correctly update RTCP metrics. If the translator changes encoding, octet count in SR packets must change. If it changes sampling rate, RTP timestamps must be adjusted. Tests verify these behaviors and that SDES CNAME items are forwarded while other SDES items may optionally be forwarded.

Mixer Testing: A mixer combines multiple sources into one stream. It generates a new SSRC for the mixed stream and includes a CSRC list identifying the contributing sources (up to 15). Receivers see CC field set to the number of contributing sources and receive CSRCs in the RTP header. Mixers generate separate RTCP reports for each side of the mix. Tests verify SSRC mixing, CSRC list correctness, and report generation for each cloud of participants.

SSRC Collision Detection: If two participants choose the same SSRC, both should send a BYE packet, leave, and rejoin with a new SSRC but the same CNAME (canonical name). Tests send a colliding RTCP report and verify the implementation sends BYE and rejoin within one minute.

SSRC Randomization: SSRC must be chosen uniformly at random over a 32-bit space. Tests collect 2500 SSRCs and place them in 25 bins. Ideally, each bin contains 100 SSRCs. With acceptable variation, each bin should have 30-50 SSRCs. Implementations with limited testing (26 samples) should have about half above and half below 2^31.
sections.eli5: Tests check if apps correctly handle translators (changing the audio format), mixers (combining multiple speakers), SSRC collisions (two apps accidentally picking the same ID), and whether they pick truly random IDs.

sections.title: Test Instrumentation and Best Practices
sections.content:
The test instrument is an application-level packet forwarder. It must be capable of sending arbitrary RTP and RTCP packets, forwarding packets between implementations with configurable delay and loss, logging packets for inspection, and measuring intervals between received packets. Control mechanisms should allow the test instrument to force sending/stopping RTP data and to terminate a session.

Successful testing requires preconfiguration of RTCP bandwidth and sender/receiver fractions. When setting packet sizes for tests, remember to include UDP and IP headers (28 bytes in IPv4). Many implementations incorrectly forget this, causing bandwidth calculations to be off.

These tests are not exhaustive. Passing all tests does not guarantee complete RTP specification conformance, but failing any test indicates a real problem. The tests illustrate common implementation errors and help ensure two implementations can work together. Different implementations should vary the test parameters to match their configurations and network conditions.
sections.eli5: The test machine needs to be able to fake packets, drop some, delay some, and measure timing carefully. Test parameters need to include network overhead, and the tests won't catch everything, but they catch the most common mistakes.
